Title: Stonebeck: calm tape, uncompensated risk

Rating: underweight

The wire was quiet and the prints came in line — precisely the conditions under which complacency compounds fastest.¹ Stonebeck's headline numbers look serene: a one_year_return of +11.0% against a ytd_return of +1.1%, drawdown flat at +0.0%. Calder & Root read this as confirmation that policy support has resolved the stress. We read the same tape as a lull between structural cracks, not evidence the cracks have closed.

Consider the spread. At 400bps, high-yield compensation sits well above the historical calm-market norm, even as policy_rate_now holds at 5.00% and cpi_now prints 2.9% — a policy stance still restrictive in real terms, whatever the disinflation narrative suggests. A spread this wide alongside a drawdown of zero is not equilibrium; it is a market pricing risk into fixed income while equity-adjacent marks have not yet caught up.² The reported_vs_public_gap of -0.2% is small, almost trivial on its face — but in our experience these gaps widen exactly when they matter most, and a negative print this early in a "quiet" cycle deserves more suspicion than comfort.

Picture the chart: a nearly flat drawdown line running alongside a stubbornly elevated spread line that refuses to converge toward it — two series that should move together in a genuinely resolved stress episode, diverging instead. That divergence is the whole thesis.

Where Calder & Root see policy support as resolution, we see policy support as a stay of execution: rates restrictive enough to keep pressure on leveraged balance sheets, spreads wide enough to admit the market agrees, and reported marks slow to reflect it.

The risk to this view: if disinflation continues and the gap between marks and reality closes benignly rather than violently, our caution simply costs carry — a plausible outcome, and the one for which "in line" prints are usually the first sign.

---
¹ Quiet sessions are when fragilities accrue their interest.
² Marks lag; spreads rarely do.
